data.turoyo: W a tre kḥayri b ḥḏoḏe, ban nawirat mparaṭṭe ak kazabat d ḥḏoḏe. U ḥa lə gməǧġəl ʕam u ḥa hul ṣafrayto.
data.translation: Die beiden blickten sich an, und mit ihren stolzen Blicken durchbohrten sie einander die Eingeweide; keiner sprach mit dem anderen.

rationale: Thin Preterit sense 1 cell: gaze as explicit instrument of the already attested figurative tearing of innards.

data.turoyo: A tre kḥayri l ḥḏoḏe ban nawirat, mparaṭṭe, u ḥa lə gməǧġəl ʕam u ḥa.
data.translation: Sie durchbohrten einer den anderen mit stolzen blicken; keiner sprach mit dem anderen.

rationale: Thin Preterit sense 1 cell: parallel gaze use with innards/object omitted; source spelling and translation casing retained.

summary: Preserve the homonym prṭ 2. Lookup confirms prṭ 1 has the same II base forms but material tearing-off/grazing examples; form identity alone is not grounds to switch entries.

The existing somatic metaphor in II.1 permits the two new figurative tearing uses without creating a hostile-look numbered sense. No claim of independent conventional idiomhood is made from two scenes in the same tale.
mparaṭṭe is a plural L-series Preterit with assimilation; the reciprocal possessor is explicit at 95/113.
Detransitive mparṭo at 65/528 describes the torn result of paper, without an agent, and is already fully represented. The inherited burning/scalding material and sense numbering are preserved.
Are the pity and hostile-gaze uses judged distinct lexical expressions by speakers, or applications of the same figurative tearing metaphor? The current evidence is kept together under II.1.
Figurative tearing of innards is not limited to pity: two linked scenes use looks as instrument and reciprocal participants; the second leaves the innards/object unexpressed.
